heading: Activation, architecture and regularization change the polysemantic-neuron share and can lower it cheaply
definition: the share of polysemantic neurons changes with the activation function, architecture or regularization (e.g. SoLU, modern convnets) and can be lowered without a large loss in performance.
summary: Several independent groups find that changing the activation, architecture or regularizer shifts neuron selectivity in toy models and small networks, though some changes leave it unchanged. Evidence is mixed on whether the share can fall without a large performance cost; SoLU itself (the activation the original paper proposed to make neurons more interpretable) has no clear independent re-test, and above 1B parameters only the original paper reports a test.

suggested_status.by_scale: Sizes behind the scales (counts: versions.V5.studies_by_size has 'not stated' 22, '<1B' 4, '1-10B' 1 and '10-100B' 2; no '>100B' key). Clause 1, 'changes with the activation function, architecture or regularization': toy models R2, from several groups (arXiv:2211.09169, arXiv:2610.20851, arXiv:2608.24007, lw:znShPqe9RdtB6AeFr, arXiv:2410.06232); the effects depend on the data regime. arXiv:2209.10652 and its web twin share authors with an original, so their toy results count as R1 and are not part of this R2. <1B and size-not-stated real nets (small transformer LMs, CNNs, audio transformers): R2, with one challenge at 1 layer (arXiv:2410.16443). Clause 2, 'can be lowered without a large loss': mixed in toys and in small real nets. It holds for some levers and not others, and is untested for the L1 CNN runs of arXiv:2501.05398 (no accuracy reported). 1-10B: ? (only rows from arXiv:2610.22127, not a test). The same study supplies the non-test probing entry at 10-100B, and the checks list rows_with_error = 25 for it, so no claim at either size should cite its rows before they are re-extracted. 10-100B: R0 (only the original: 33% to 42% at 64 layers, about 50B; its Discussion also reports a 'very strong gain at 12 billion parameters'). >100B: no data. The SoLU example: R0 on verdict-bearing evidence at every scale (only the original). At toy and small or unstated sizes, other groups report SoLU results that carry no V5 verdict and point both ways (see reason), so it is ? there until they are judged.
suggested_status.reason:
counts: versions.V5.verdicts gives supports.studies 17, limits_scope.studies 19 and challenges.studies 1; versions.V5.studies_supports_only = 2. These keys were built before the checks and have not been rebuilt. They still include two limits_scope verdicts that the checks say should be none: 10.1073/pnas.2216698120 l2 (DD-10 first-layer kernel size; its limits_scope on the DeepSEA regularization route stands) and arXiv:2406.16990 l1 (training-strategy confound; its supports verdict then becomes its only V5 verdict). Re-quote the keys once the verdict fixes reach the records and the counts are rebuilt. The flagged V5 row errors also remain in the row records: arXiv:2610.20851#r5–#r8, where 'updates=106' means 10^6 updates, and arXiv:2501.05398#r03, where the reader gave VGG-13's 83.3/83.7 for ResNet34. This status quotes no rows_by_state key and none of these rows' values, and no fix removes a supports verdict the level rests on.

Clause 1, 'changes with the activation function, architecture or regularization' (R2 in toys and small nets). Changing the architecture or training changes neuron-selectivity measures in studies from groups other than the original's (none is marked SAME GROUP in the studies index):
- small transformer LMs: arXiv:2611.03655 (specificity 0.523 vs 0.375 at lower CE), arXiv:2610.19907 (AutoInterp 0.866 vs 0.605/0.667), arXiv:2410.16443 (gains at 2L, 3L and 6L on all three metrics, and at 12L on Random-only)
- CNNs: arXiv:2501.05398 (L1: 91.5 to 67.0), 10.1073/pnas.2216698120
- synthetic MLPs: arXiv:2608.24007
The one challenge is CRATE-1L, which scores below GPT-2 on all metrics. Some interventions leave the measure unchanged: the TopoLoss regularizer in ViT-S/16 (arXiv:2609.24379), and post-hoc Wanda weight pruning with 2-epoch fine-tuning of DeiT-III B/16 at 10-70% sparsity, which is a structural intervention, not a regularizer (arXiv:2603.15919).

Same-group evidence: counts: versions.V5.tested_sharing_an_author_with_an_original = 1. That study is arXiv:2209.10652 (Toy Models of Superposition), the only V5-tested study marked SAME GROUP in the studies index; its author list shares authors with an original. Its web twin (web:https://transformer-circuits.pub/2022/toy_model/index.html, V5 limits_scope only) is the same paper. It carries no flag in the index, but it is same-group too. Their L1 and adversarial-training results count as the original group's extension (R1), and the R2 above does not rest on them.

Clause 2, 'can be lowered without a large loss': mixed. Some levers report no large loss: arXiv:2611.03655 (evaluation CE 2.417 vs dense 2.452), 10.1073/pnas.2216698120 (AUPRC improves for BD-10/DD-10, no numbers in text), arXiv:2602.12403 (accuracy equal or higher at the best λ, with an added layer) and arXiv:2410.06232 (negligible loss in a 25-unit toy). Costs are reported in arXiv:2410.16443 (CRATE validation loss about 0.2–0.35 nats worse than GPT-2 at small sizes), arXiv:2505.00509, arXiv:2610.19907 and arXiv:2511.13653; MoWE is also 0.197 nats worse than standard MoE (arXiv:2611.03655). In toys, dropout lowers superposition with an unquantified performance loss that extra compute does not close (lw:znShPqe9RdtB6AeFr). The clause is untested for the largest real-net reductions, the L1 runs of arXiv:2501.05398 (ResNet34 91.5 to 67.0, VGG-13 (BN) 84.8 to 71.8), which report no accuracy.

SoLU, the version's own example: no verdict-bearing re-test (counts: versions.V5.tested_by_tranche.T1 = 0). Among V5 tests, arXiv:2211.09169 attempted SoLU but got no clear results. Studies with no V5 verdict (relation uses_without_test or discusses) do report SoLU results. They are coverage, not support or against, and they point both ways:
- arXiv:2503.07639 (reviewed; chess GPT-2-like models at matched active parameters): SoLU scores below GELU on board-state coverage and reconstruction (arXiv:2503.07639#tbl1-solu-cov, arXiv:2503.07639#tbl1-solu-rec). This is a board-state alignment proxy, not a share of polysemantic neurons.
- lw:wMn9wSxzSs3uHiAmu (informal; toy superposition model): SoLU gives less superposition at high sparsity, and loss stays in a narrow 10^-4 to 10^-3 range across activation functions (lw:wMn9wSxzSs3uHiAmu#f0).
- lw:S76fyabDPySQgh9G3 (informal; same author as lw:wMn9wSxzSs3uHiAmu): without LayerNorm, SoLU gives more superposition than softmax in the toy autoencoder (lw:S76fyabDPySQgh9G3#f1, row lw:S76fyabDPySQgh9G3#r4). The original's SoLU models add an extra LayerNorm.
- arXiv:2507.15798 (reviewed; SoLU in low-parameter vision bottlenecks): feature-map channel alignment (Oij) changes under SoLU in MobileNetv3 and Batch-Norm MobileNeXt but stays similar in ConvNeXt, and the pack line does not say how Oij maps onto polysemanticity. SoLU's accuracy cost runs from about 1% (ConvNeXt) to nearly 50% (Inverted Bottlenecks) (arXiv:2507.15798#f0, arXiv:2507.15798#f1).
- arXiv:2304.12918 and arXiv:2305.19911 (N2G, likely the same work, both SAME GROUP): one SoLU-model neuron's graph splits into Dutch, English and Swedish subgraphs. This single qualitative case shows that polysemantic neurons remain in SoLU models; it says nothing about a change in their share, and as same-group work it is R1 at most.
Above 1B, only the original reports a test (counts: versions.V5.coverage_by_operation.training.by_size '10-100B': 1), and its gain is smaller at 64 layers.
suggested_status.open_questions:
Results that would change the level:
- V5 verdicts on the studies with SoLU results that have none: arXiv:2503.07639, lw:wMn9wSxzSs3uHiAmu, lw:S76fyabDPySQgh9G3 and arXiv:2507.15798 (other groups), and arXiv:2304.12918 / arXiv:2305.19911 (same group, R1 at most). Depending on those verdicts, the SoLU example at toy and small or unstated sizes would move from ? (R0 on verdict-bearing evidence, only the original) toward R2, or toward C in the settings where SoLU did worse. No verdict-bearing study re-tests SoLU vs baseline in a language model with blinded rating at matched loss (T1 = 0).
- Any architecture or regularizer test at 1-10B or above on a named LLM family. Today only the original covers 10-100B: a 'very strong gain' at 12B, but 33% to 42% at 64 layers (50B).
- Matched-loss comparisons that report an actual share of polysemantic neurons rather than proxy scores.
- For the 'without a large loss' clause: task performance for the L1 runs of arXiv:2501.05398, the largest real-net reductions, which report none.
- Whether the CRATE-1L reversal, or the no-change results for TopoLoss and Wanda pruning, extend to the levers the version names. If so, those parts would move toward C.

source.title: Softmax Linear Units
source.authors: Nelson Elhage; Tristan Hume; Catherine Olsson; Neel Nanda; Tom Henighan; Scott Johnston; Sheer El Showk; Nicholas Joseph; Nova DasSarma; Ben Mann; Danny Hernandez; Amanda Askell; Kamal Ndousse; Andy Jones; Dawn Drain; Anna Chen; Yuntao Bai; Deep Ganguli; Liane Lovitt; Zac Hatfield-Dodds; Jackson Kernion; Tom Conerly; Shauna Kravec; Stanislav Fort; Saurav Kadavath; Josh Jacobson; Eli Tran-Johnson; Jared Kaplan; Jack Clark; Tom Brown; Sam McCandlish; Dario Amodei; Christopher Olah

original_result.setup: They swapped the MLP activation for SoLU plus an extra LayerNorm in transformers of 1 to 64 layers, and blinded raters judged 60 neurons per model.
original_result.result: About 60% of SoLU neurons were rated interpretable versus about 35% in baseline models, with a smaller gain at 64 layers (42% vs 33%); in a 16-layer model, an extra LayerNorm alone gave about half of SoLU's gain. Loss stayed within about 0.01 nats of baseline, so SoLU models performed like baseline models 0.95 to 1.05 times their size.
original_result.interpretation: This is the displayed original-result block, not a guarantee that the original tested every part of this claim.

sources.headline: L1 regularization removed superposition in toy models; adversarial training reduced it.
Training and architecture choices raised monosemanticity in toy models at comparable or better loss.
Deeper genomic CNNs with small kernels suppressed DNA-motif mixing in neurons, while prediction AUPRC improved.
The per-layer share of uninterpretable neurons differed between supervised AST and BEATs variants, all audio transformers.
Widening Boolean-task networks at a fixed parameter count roughly doubled their feature capacity and raised accuracy.
Fine-tuning with the MonoLoss penalty made example units single-concept, without accuracy loss at the best weight.
MLP neurons' selectivity for single data clusters varied strongly across activation functions; ReGLU gave the highest.
TopK-sparse transformer neurons scored higher on automated interpretability (AutoInterp) than loss- or width-matched dense ones.
Dropout reduced superposition in toy autoencoders, spreading features over more dimensions.
Around a single sparsity level, low-bit BitLinear toy models showed later, weaker superposition than dense ones.
Energy constraints split mixed units into groups for identity ('what') and position ('where'), at negligible loss.
Neurons of CRATE, a sparse-coding transformer, got higher interpretability scores than GPT-2's at several model depths.
Polysemanticity varied with architecture and fell with an L1 sparsity loss in ResNet34 and batch-norm VGG-13.
Training-time self-ablation narrowed neuron responses in higher transformer layers, judged by token-diversity and entropy proxies.
Weight-sparse transformers spread concepts much less than dense models across nodes that also serve other tasks.
Weight decay raised a sparse-ReLU encoder's unit–feature alignment (median MCC) from 0.878 to 0.987–0.993.
MoWE native coordinates were more specific than dense ones at equal or better loss.
L1 removed toy-model superposition only at higher loss; adversarial training, only with implausibly large attacks.
Loss was slightly worse than the baseline at middle widths; widening for monosemanticity cost extra compute.
In the genomic CNN DeepSEA, strong regularization suppressed DNA-motif mixing but left many dead neurons.
AST–BEATs gaps in uninterpretable neurons cannot be tied to training alone; architecture and pretraining also differ.
ResNet depth changed polysemanticity only slightly; the trend reversed when example patches were picked by activation.
Applying MonoLoss directly to the backbone's last layer overfit the model to a fixed image subset.
The ranking of activation functions by neuron selectivity for data clusters changed with the data's geometry.
Pruning DeiT-III weights with Wanda caused no consistent change in neuron selectivity or class-label entropy.
The TopK-sparse transformer matched dense loss only with an MLP eight times the dense width.
Dropout's lower superposition came with a performance loss that extra compute did not close.
Low-bit BitLinear and dense toy networks behaved alike except within narrow ranges of feature sparsity.
CRATE's interpretability edge over GPT-2 shrank in some settings and came with higher loss.
Sparsity loss and dropout left polysemanticity nearly unchanged in several vision models.
Self-ablation did not narrow lower-layer neurons and raised validation perplexity by 13–22%.
Weight sparsity traded capability for interpretability, and complex-task circuits stayed partly polysemantic.
Training ViT-S/16 with TopoLoss, a loss that arranges neurons topographically, left neuron monosemanticity essentially unchanged.
With weight decay on, swapping the output activation function barely changed unit–feature alignment (MCC).
MoWE's more readable units cost 0.197 nats more evaluation cross-entropy than a standard MoE.
L1 removed superposition only at higher loss; adversarial training, only with attacks of 80% input norm.
In one-layer models, CRATE neurons scored below GPT-2's on every interpretability metric tested.

counting_note: Each group counts distinct sources for this claim. The same source can appear in more than one group or claim; counts are not votes.

untested.what: SoLU, the version's own example, and the original's blinded human rating are not re-tested by any other study. arXiv:2211.09169 attempted SoLU but got no clear results.
untested.basis: counts: versions.V5.tested_by_tranche.T1 = 0. The untested-parts lines of arXiv:2211.09169, arXiv:2209.10652, arXiv:2610.19907, arXiv:2611.03655, arXiv:2608.24007 and arXiv:2609.24379 all list SoLU as not tested.

untested.what: Above 1B parameters, only the original tests a lever, and it carries no verdict. It trains baseline and SoLU models from 1L to 64L (~50B) in steps of about 4x in parameters, and rates interpretability at 1L, 16L, 24L, 40L and 64L. At ~50B it reports 42% (SoLU) vs 33% (baseline) interpretable (Section 6.2). Its Discussion reports a 'very strong gain at 12 billion parameters', so its 1L–40L group (~35% to ~60% interpretable) includes a model above 1B. Section 6 gives a size only for the 64L model; the 12B model is most likely the 40L. No verdict-bearing test covers models above 1B parameters, and none covers models above 100B.
untested.basis: counts: versions.V5.coverage_by_operation.training.by_size has '10-100B': 1, which is the original (TITLE:Softmax Linear Units, row R3). Its 12B and ~50B models both fall in this bin; the sizes come from the check of Section 6.2 and the Discussion. coverage_by_operation.measurement.by_size has only 'not stated' and '<1B'. coverage_by_operation.probing.by_size '1-10B': 1 and '10-100B': 1 come from arXiv:2610.22127, which the verdict marks NOT A TEST. versions.V5.studies_by_size has no '>100B' key.

untested.what: No test uses a named production LLM family. Every tested study's family is 'other or not stated'.
untested.basis: counts: versions.V5.studies_by_family gives OLMo 1, Qwen 1 and Mistral 1, all under coverage_by_operation.probing.by_family. That probing comes only from arXiv:2610.22127 (NOT A TEST, k-sparse probing of OLMoE, OLMo2, Qwen, Qwen2.5, Mixtral and Llama13 neurons). 'other or not stated': 23.

untested.what: Standard regularizers (dropout, weight decay, L1 on activations) are varied only in toy models, CNNs and one ViT (TopoLoss), never in a transformer language model with polysemanticity measured.
untested.basis: Rows of lw:znShPqe9RdtB6AeFr, arXiv:2610.20851, arXiv:2209.10652, arXiv:2501.05398 and arXiv:2609.24379. The untested-parts lines of arXiv:2610.19907 and arXiv:2611.03655 (regularization not tested) and of arXiv:2410.16443 (regularization not isolated).

untested.what: The largest polysemanticity reductions measured in real vision nets (L1 λ=80: ResNet34 91.5 to 67.0, VGG-13 (BN) 84.8 to 71.8) come with no reported accuracy, so the 'without a large loss' clause is untested for them.
untested.basis: Verdict reason for arXiv:2501.05398 (performance cost is not reported) and its untested-parts line (task performance or accuracy cost of lowering polysemanticity).

wording_issues.issue: Few studies report a share. The original reports the fraction rated interpretable (~35% to ~60%). Others report the percentage of uninterpretable neurons (AND, figure only), the fraction with Mu > 0.5 (0.26% at α=0 in ViT-S), or a share over specialized neurons only (arXiv:2608.24007, per the verdict fix on T1-R2). Most results are mean proxy scores instead: AutoInterp (0.866 for ST), coordinate specificity (MoWE), SemanticLens score %, MCC axis alignment, superposition geometry, feature capacity, CPE. arXiv:2511.13653 and arXiv:2611.03655 state that they report no share of polysemantic neurons.

wording_issues.phrase: can be lowered without a large loss in performance
wording_issues.issue: This depends on the lever. Some show no large loss: MoWE CE 2.417 vs dense 2.452; better AUPRC for BD-10/DD-10; MonoLoss accuracy equal or higher with an added layer; negligible loss in a 25-unit toy. Others carry costs: CRATE 0.2–0.35 nats worse than GPT-2; self-ablation perplexity 5.73 to 6.47–6.97; ST needs 8× MLP width to match dense M=4 loss; MoWE is 0.197 nats worse than standard MoE; weight sparsity needs 100–1000x compute (text); toy L1 and dropout cost loss.

Only the original tests SoLU. It reports ~35% to ~60% interpretable at 1–40 layers, but 33% to 42% at 64 layers (50B). A LayerNorm-only control lands about halfway at 16L, so part of the gain is the extra LayerNorm. No other study in the pack tests SoLU.

No study compares convnet generations. The nearest results: narrow ResNet18 is more polysemantic than broader models, and ViTs are high (SemanticLens r02; ViT only in the figure text). ResNet50, 101 and 152 give CPE of about 0.8418, 0.8458 and 0.8467, a ~0.005 rise that reverses under activation-based selection. PURE's ResNet-34 vs deeper ResNet comparison is hedged and deferred (row r2, no V5 verdict). Several studies list modern convnets as untested.

wording_issues.phrase: changes with the activation function, architecture or regularization
wording_issues.issue: Not every change moves it, and the direction varies. Unchanged: TopoLoss (Mu 0.2340 to 0.2359, n.s.), Wanda pruning, dropout in three of four CNNs, L1 in ResNet50 and VGG-13. Reversed: CRATE-1L is below GPT-2 on all metrics; self-ablation raises entropy in L0 and L3; dropout in the dense, varying-importance toy regime makes room for more superposition. Whether and which way it changes depends on the base architecture, the layer and the data regime.

Apart from the original's SoLU in real LMs, only synthetic MLPs and encoders vary the activation. There the ranking depends on data geometry (ReLU 65.74% vs 99.50% with Mj > 1/2) and on weight decay: at wd 0.03, ReLU, LeakyReLU and linear outputs give MCC 0.994, 0.987 and 0.968.

Many supporting results measure something other than neurons that respond to unrelated inputs. Toy studies measure superposition geometry (L1, dropout, BitLinear) or MCC axis alignment. arXiv:2510.04500 measures feature capacity. MoWE scores native FFN-update output coordinates, not hidden neurons.

method_sensitivity.what: The original's SoLU gain is ~35% to ~60% interpretable at 1–40 layers but 33% to 42% at 64 layers. CRATE is reversed at 1L (Top-and-Random 3.9 vs 8.8), large at 2L (8.05 vs 4.2) and small at 12L (6.8 vs 6.34).

In the original, the strict annotator gives ~20% (baseline) vs ~60% (SoLU), against about 40% vs 60% for the other two. For CRATE at 2L, Random-only gives 6.95 vs 1.95 but the Anthropic metric gives 11.35 vs 10.2.

method_sensitivity.factor: layer (and, within a layer, the selectivity metric)
method_sensitivity.what: Self-ablating GPT-Neo on TinyStories: in L4–L7, N2G token diversity falls (e.g. 8 to 5 at L7). In L0–L3, token diversity and neuron entropy show no narrowing (6 to 7 at L3; entropy 2.08 to 2.38 at L0). But Table 2's other N2G measures (not in rows) fall in L0–L3 as well: graph density (e.g. L3 0.443 to 0.070), which the paper reads as more selective neurons, and edges to activation (e.g. L2 1.57 to 0.17). So whether lower layers change depends on the metric. In Basset, L2 shows almost no synonymous-motif mixture while L3 shows substantial mixture. In AST on ESC50, the share of uninterpretable neurons falls from shallow to deep blocks (Fig 6, figure only).

method_sensitivity.factor: base architecture under the same intervention
method_sensitivity.what: With L1 at λ=80, ResNet34 drops from 91.5 to 67.0 but ResNet50 only from 89.3 to 87.7. Dropout lowers only VGG-13 (BN) (84.7 to 78.4). Task complexity (binary vs 26-class) raises the score in ResNet50 (87.1 to 89.2) and VGG-13 (BN) (82.7 to 84.6) but lowers it in VGG-13 (85.3 to 83.1).

method_sensitivity.factor: data geometry / feature sparsity and importance
method_sensitivity.what: ReLU's share of specialized neurons with Mj > 1/2 is 65.74 ± 1.69% in the axis-aligned setting and 99.50 ± 0.08% in the non-orthogonal setting. Dropout solely reduces superposition with uniform importance, but with dense features of decaying importance it leaves room for more.

method_sensitivity.factor: weight decay, learning rate and readout
method_sensitivity.what: In the sparse-ReLU exact-capacity encoder, median MCC after 10^6 updates is 0.878 at wd 0 and 0.987 at wd 0.03. Removing weight decay from the reference gives 0.829 ± 0.029 vs 0.994. Under entropy SD 2 nats, a bias-free readout gives MCC 0.662 ± 0.009 vs 0.962 ± 0.002 for an affine readout. In the toy absolute-value task with initial bias −1, a negative bias alone does not robustly give mostly monosemantic models: either a high learning rate (Fig 22, text, not in rows) or a low bias weight-decay rate (Fig 23) is needed.

CoE's ResNet depth trend (about 0.005 CPE) reverses under activation-based instead of relevance-based patch selection. In MoWE, dense native coordinates score the same as a random rotation (0.375 vs 0.375), while MoWE native coordinates score 0.523. In the separate 10-layer, d=768 pilot (MoWE 162.5M and dense 72.7M parameters, about 5B tokens; layer 6, 500 coordinates), purity is 0.3763 for MoWE vs 0.2973 for dense. That purity is an earlier diagnostic the authors say not to compare with final specificity.

TopoLoss accuracy is 0.612 at α=0, 0.614 at α=0.1 and 0.596 at α=1.0, while Mu stays flat at all three. Dropout p=0.4 is described as aggressive and p=0.15 as intermediate in both performance and superposition. The weight-sparse study's method-sensitivity line says activation sparsity is non-monotonic on the capability-interpretability frontier (Figure 37, not in rows).

status_amendment.public_note: The status now treats the claim in two parts: independent groups find that architecture and training change measures of neuron polysemanticity in toy models and small networks, while evidence that it can be lowered without a large performance cost is mixed. It also lists SoLU results from other studies that have not yet been assessed and point both ways, so SoLU's own status at small sizes is now uncertain, and it counts Toy Models of Superposition as work by the original authors' group; the overall level is unchanged.
